entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11184"/><div sID="gen20177" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11184"/>6. Though God so threatened the people for their idolatry (<reference osisRef="Ezek.14.5">Eze 14:5</reference>), yet He would rather they should avert the calamity by "repentance."<div eID="gen20177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20178" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">turn yourselves--</hi>Calvin translates, "turn others" (namely, the stranger proselytes in the land). As ye have been the advisers of others (see <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.7">Eze 14:7</reference>, "the stranger that sojourneth in Israel") to idolatry, so bestow at least as much pains in turning them to the truth; the surest proof of repentance. But the parallelism to <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.3">Eze 14:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.4">4</reference> favors English Version. Their sin was twofold: (1) "In their heart" or inner man; (2) "Put before their face," that is, exhibited outwardly. So their repentance is generally expressed by "repent," and is then divided into: (1) "Turn yourselves (inwardly) from your idols"; (2) "Turn away your faces (outwardly) from all your abominations." It is not likely that an exhortation to convert others should come between the two affecting themselves. <div eID="gen20178" type="x-p"/>

Fairbairn translates, as it is the same Hebrew as in the previous clause, "concerning Me," it is natural that God should use the same expression in His reply as was used in the consultation of Him. I the Lord have deceived that prophet--</hi>not directly, but through Satan and his ministers; not merely permissively, but by overruling their evil to serve the purposes of His righteous judgment, to be a touchstone to separate the precious from the vile, and to "prove" His people (<reference osisRef="Deut.13.3">De 13:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.23">1Ki 22:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.4.10">Jr 4:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.11">2Th 2:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.12">12</reference>). Evil comes not from God, though God overrules it to serve His will (<reference osisRef="Job.12.16">Job 12:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.1.3">Jas 1:3</reference>). This declaration of God is intended to answer their objection, "Jeremiah and Ezekiel are but two opposed to the many prophets who announce 'peace' to us." "Nay, deceive not yourselves, those prophets of yours are deluding you, and I permit them to do so as a righteous judgment on your wilful blindness." <div eID="gen20184" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11188"/><div sID="gen20185" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11188"/>10. As they dealt deceitfully with God by seeking answers of peace without repentance, so God would let them be dealt with deceitfully by the prophets whom they consulted. God would chastise their sin with a corresponding sin; as they rejected the safe directions of the true light, He would send the pernicious delusions of a false one; prophets would be given them who should re-echo the deceitfulness that already wrought in their own bosom, to their ruin [Fairbairn]. The people had themselves alone to blame, for they were long ago forewarned how to discern and to treat a false prophet (<reference osisRef="Deut.13.3">De 13:3</reference>); the very existence of such deceivers among them was a sign of God's judicial displeasure (compare in Saul's case, <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.14">1Sa 16:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.6">28:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.7">7</reference>). They and the prophet, being dupes of a common delusion, should be involved in a common ruin. <div eID="gen20185" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11190"/><div sID="gen20187" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11190"/>12. The second part of the chapter: the effect which the presence of a few righteous persons was to have on the purposes of God (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.18.24-Gen.18.32">Ge 18:24-32</reference>). God had told Jeremiah that the guilt of Judah was too great to be pardoned even for the intercession of Moses and Samuel (<reference osisRef="Ps.99.6">Psa 99:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.14.2">Jr 14:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.15.1">15:1</reference>), which had prevailed formerly (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.11-Exod.32.14">Ex 32:11-14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.14.13-Num.14.20">Nu 14:13-20</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.8-1Sam.7.12">1Sa 7:8-12</reference>), implying the extraordinary heinousness of their guilt, since in ordinary cases "the effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man (for others) availeth much" (<reference osisRef="Jas.5.16">Jas 5:16</reference>). Ezekiel supplements Jeremiah by adding that not only those two once successful intercessors, but not even the three pre-eminently righteous men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, could stay God's judgments by their righteousness. <div eID="gen20187" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 12. The second part of the chapter: the effect which the presence of a few righteous persons was to have on the purposes of God (compare Ge 18:24-32 ). Ezekiel supplements Jeremiah by adding that not only those two once successful intercessors, but not even the three pre-eminently righteous men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, could stay God's judgments by their righteousness.

Noah, Daniel ... Job--</hi>specified in particular as having been saved from overwhelming calamities for their personal righteousness. Noah had the members of his family alone given to him, amidst the general wreck. Daniel saved from the fury of the king of Babylon the three youths (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.17">Da 2:17</reference>, 18, 48, 49). Though his prophecies mostly were later than those of Ezekiel, his fame for piety and wisdom was already established, and the events recorded in <reference osisRef="Dan.1.1-Dan.2.49">Da 1:1-2:49</reference> had transpired. The Jews would naturally, in their fallen condition, pride themselves on one who reflected such glory on his nation at the heathen capital, and would build vain hopes (here set aside) on his influence in averting ruin from them. Thus the objection to the authenticity of Daniel from this passage vanishes. "Job" forms the climax (and is therefore put out of chronological order), having not even been left a son or a daughter, and having had himself to pass through an ordeal of suffering before his final deliverance, and therefore forming the most simple instance of the righteousness of God, which would save the righteous themselves alone in the nation, and that after an ordeal of suffering, but not spare even a son or daughter for their sake (<reference osisRef="Ezek.14.16">Eze 14:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.20">18, 20</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Jer.7.16">Jr 7:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.11.14">11:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.14.11">14:11</reference>).<div eID="gen20189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20190" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">deliver ... souls by ... righteousness--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.11.4">Pr 11:4</reference>); not the righteousness of works, but that of grace, a truth less clearly understood under the law (<reference osisRef="Rom.4.3">Ro 4:3</reference>). <div eID="gen20190" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11193"/><div sID="gen20191" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11193"/>15-21. The argument is cumulative. He first puts the case of the land sinning so as to fall under the judgment of a famine (<reference osisRef="Ezek.14.13">Eze 14:13</reference>); then (<reference osisRef="Ezek.14.15">Eze 14:15</reference>) "noisome beasts" (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.22">Le 26:22</reference>); then "the sword"; then, worst of all, "pestilence." The three most righteous of men should deliver only themselves in these several four cases. In <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.21">Eze 14:21</reference> he concentrates the whole in one mass of condemnation. If Noah, Daniel, Job, could not deliver the land, when deserving only one judgment, "how much more" when all four judgments combined are justly to visit the land for sin, shall these three righteous men not deliver it. <div eID="gen20191" type="x-p"/>

Yet ... a remnant--</hi>not of righteous persons, but some of the guilty who should "come forth" from the destruction of Jerusalem to Babylon, to lead a life of hopeless exile there. The reference here is to judgment, not mercy, as <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.23">Eze 14:23</reference> shows.<div eID="gen20194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20195" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye shall see their ... doings; and ... be comforted--</hi>Ye, the exiles at the Chebar, who now murmur at God's judgment about to be inflicted on Jerusalem as harsh, when ye shall see the wicked "ways" and character of the escaped remnant, shall acknowledge that both Jerusalem and its inhabitants deserved their fate; his recognition of the righteousness of the judgment will reconcile you to it, and so ye shall be "comforted" under it [Calvin]. Then would follow mercy to the elect remnant, though that is not referred to here, but in <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.43">Eze 20:43</reference>. <div eID="gen20195" type="x-p"/>
